Push-Pull.short_definition: Swinging between closeness and distance in repeating cycles, so the other person keeps working to get back to the warm stretch.
Push-Pull.core_meaning: Swinging between closeness and distance in repeating cycles, so the other person keeps working to get back to the warm stretch.
Push-Pull.expanded_definition: Push-pull is a rhythm in a close relationship: a run of attention, plans and affection, then a sudden cooling with no clear reason, then a return to warmth. One cold week means little, since everyone has them. What marks it is a swing that repeats, a cold phase that tends to start right after you got close or asked for something, and a warm phase that comes back mainly when you pull away or work harder.
Push-Pull.plain_language_summary: Someone is very close, then suddenly distant, then close again, and you end up spending your energy trying to get back to the good part.
Push-Pull.why_this_matters: You start organizing your attention around a temperature you cannot predict, and you tend to read every cold spell as something you must have caused. That can crowd out your own plans, friendships and sleep.
what_it_is: A repeating swing between a warm phase (daily contact, future talk, tenderness) and a cool phase (short replies, vague plans, slow answers).
Cool phases that arrive without a stated reason, so you are left guessing what you did.
Warmth that tends to come back when you pull away, make other plans, or stop asking for more.
A rhythm that runs across months, which is what separates it from one bad week.
what_it_sounds_like: Three days of good-morning texts and plans for the weekend, then no reply until Thursday night.
"I've just been really busy," said with no mention of the plans that were dropped.
"I missed you so much," arriving the day after you finally went out with friends.
"I'm not sure what I want right now," followed two weeks later by "Why are you being so distant?"
A warm voice call at midnight after a week of one-word texts, and no mention of the week.
"Don't read into it. I'm just like this sometimes."
what_it_is_not: A person who goes quiet under real pressure, such as a death in the family, an illness, or a work crunch, and tells you so.
An introvert who needs regular solitary time and says so plainly, with a predictable rhythm you can plan around.
Two people early in dating who are still working out how much contact suits each of them.
Ambivalence that is stated openly: 'I'm unsure about this' is hard to hear but is an honest message, not a cycle.
A relationship with a real distance difference, such as shift work or time zones, where the gaps follow the schedule.
this_may_be_it_when: The cool phases start soon after a moment of real closeness, such as an intimate talk or a weekend away.
Warmth returns in step with your pulling back, not in step with anything happening in their life.
You can tell the day's mood from the first message, and you plan your own week around it.
Asking what changed gets 'nothing' or 'you're overthinking', and the cycle begins again.
You have been through at least three or four full swings, not one.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The quiet spells line up with something you can see, such as a work deadline or a family event.
They tell you ahead of time: 'I'll be off my phone this week, I'll call Sunday.' And they call.
The swings are small, and both of you move through them with no one chasing.
When you name the gap, they explain it and the next one is shorter or better flagged.
You are the one who tends to go cold, and they are simply responding to that.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone managing depression, anxiety or burnout can swing in how much contact they can manage, without being aware of the effect on you.
A person afraid of commitment may approach and retreat out of their own fear, which is painful for you even though it is not about controlling you.
Life events such as a new job, a child, or a sick parent legitimately change availability from week to week.
common_false_positives: Early dating where one of you is slower to commit and the contact is uneven for a few weeks.
A long-distance relationship in which busy periods at work thin out the calls.
A friend who disappears for months at a time because that is how they treat everyone, not only you.
discernment_questions: Can you predict when the cool phase will start, and does it follow closeness or following a request from you?
Does the warmth return because something changed for them, or because you backed off?
Do you spend more time decoding their silence than doing the things you used to enjoy?
When you ask directly about a cold spell, do you get an answer you can use?
Would you describe the relationship to a friend as one steady thing, or as a series of weathers?
less_concerning_if: They name their own pattern and say what they are doing about it, such as asking for notice before they go quiet.
The cool phases are short and the closeness comes back without you chasing.
You can tell them it unsettles you and they are curious about that, not irritated.
more_concerning_if: The cold phases grow longer or sharper each cycle, and the warm ones need more effort from you.
Cooling follows your attempts to see other people or spend time on your own plans.
The distance is combined with criticism, comparisons, or hints that someone else would be easier.
pattern_over_time_signs: You stop making plans more than a day ahead, since you do not know which version of them will turn up.
You send more messages in the cold phases and fewer in the warm ones, as if on a leash.
Friends comment that you check your phone constantly or seem anxious in a way you did not before.
The warm stretches are shorter than they used to be, yet they still feel worth waiting for.
Push-Pull.repair_check: Change here looks like steadier contact over months, plus a straight answer whenever they do need space: when they will be back in touch and why. A passionate reunion that resets everything, with the silence still unmentioned, only restarts the loop.
Push-Pull.boundary_respect_check: A week on from asking for steadier contact, what does the calendar show? Contact that really steadies is a good sign. Warmth that lasts only while you keep quiet, with the cool phase creeping back as you ease off, is an answer to your request too.
Push-Pull.psychological_mechanism: Closeness that comes and goes can make people watch for signs of the next change. When warmth returns after a gap, the relief can feel stronger than steady kindness would, which may tie a person more tightly to the one who gave it. Uncertainty tends to keep attention fixed on the relationship, and people often fill the unexplained gaps with self-blame.
Push-Pull.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constant low-level alertness around their phone, rehearsing messages, and putting friends and hobbies aside in case the warm phase arrives. Some say they began to feel they were too much when closeness was offered and not enough when it was taken away. Many describe confusion about whether the good moments or the bad ones were the real relationship.

response_options.soft_clarification: Describe what you notice without guessing at reasons: 'Some weeks we talk every day and some weeks I hear nothing. Can you tell me what's going on at your end?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say what you will and will not do: 'I'm not available to wait through silences. If you need space, tell me how long, or I'll take it as an answer.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying within minutes during cool phases, return to your own plans, and notice how you feel when no one is setting the pace.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a friend the last two months of messages and ask what shape they see. Outsiders often spot the rhythm quicker than the person inside it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this is a colleague or supervisor who is friendly one week and cold the next, keep a dated note of what was said and ask in writing for clear expectations on your projects.

Push-Pull.boundary_script: "I like you, and I can't do the hot-and-cold. Talking every few days at an ordinary pace works for me, and so does a heads-up when you need a break. If that doesn't suit you, I'll step back."
Push-Pull.safety_note: Alone, this rhythm is a source of distress, not physical danger. It becomes more serious if cold phases turn into threats, if you are told you will be abandoned for ordinary things such as seeing family, or if money or housing depends on their mood. Then tell one trusted person what is happening and speak to a counselor about making a plan that does not rely on their moods.
misuse_warning: Pinning the label on someone who is slow to text or who has real ambivalence can turn an honest 'I'm unsure' into a charge of manipulation.
Naming it in the middle of an argument as proof of a hidden game tends to shut down the very conversation that would clarify things.
Push-Pull.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Compared with Love Bombing, which front-loads affection and need never cool, this has real distance in it. Hoovering comes after a split or a long gap, when someone reappears with promises. Breadcrumbing is thin, steady scraps with no warm phase at all. Push-pull has both: real stretches of closeness, then real distance, again and again.

Intermittent Reinforcement.short_definition: Handing out affection, praise or kindness unpredictably and rarely, so that the few good moments hold a person more tightly than steady warmth would.
Intermittent Reinforcement.core_meaning: Handing out affection, praise or kindness unpredictably and rarely, so that the few good moments hold a person more tightly than steady warmth would.
Intermittent Reinforcement.expanded_definition: The name comes from learning research on reward schedules, where rewards that arrive on an unpredictable timetable tend to produce persistent effort. In a relationship, it describes long stretches of criticism, indifference or flat routine broken by occasional real warmth or praise. Every relationship has good and bad days, so the pattern is judged by ratio and timing: how rare the good moments are, how much you do to earn them, and how hard they are to predict.
Intermittent Reinforcement.plain_language_summary: Kindness shows up only now and then, with no way of knowing when, so you keep working for the next bit and it becomes hard to leave.
Intermittent Reinforcement.why_this_matters: Effort goes up while the returns go down. The rarity of the good moments is what makes them feel worth waiting for, so the loop can feed itself, and you may end up measuring the whole relationship by its best hour.
what_it_is: A relationship where approval or tenderness arrives on no schedule you can learn, while criticism or neglect fills the gaps.
Rewards that are real but small in number, such as a compliment, a surprise visit, or a night when they are fully attentive.
A rising effort on your side: more chores, more patience, more worry about getting it right.
A pattern that can occur at home, at work, in friendships, and in families.
what_it_sounds_like: Weeks of 'fine' and 'whatever you want,' then one evening of "You're the best thing in my life."
A supervisor who ignores your reports for months and then praises you in front of the team.
"See, this is how it could always be, if you tried a bit harder."
A parent who is cold through most of a visit and then hugs you tightly at the door.
Silence when you do well, and a thank-you only when you stay late or give up something you wanted.
"I do love you. You just don't see it."
what_it_is_not: A relationship with ordinary variation in mood, where kind days are still the large majority.
A partner or boss who is consistently reserved, and shows appreciation in small, steady ways that do not look like praise.
A season of grief, illness or overwhelm in which the other person has less warmth to give.
A family culture that rarely says 'I love you' aloud but shows it reliably through actions.
A pleasant surprise after a difficult period of real conflict, with an honest conversation attached.
this_may_be_it_when: You cannot guess which of your actions earns the good moment, or whether any of them do.
The warm episodes are far outnumbered by cold or critical ones, and you still describe the relationship by the warm ones.
You find yourself doing more and more, for rewards that stay the same size or shrink.
Praise tends to come when you are on the edge of leaving, going quiet, or giving up.
You feel a rush of relief and gratitude at small kindnesses that would barely register elsewhere.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can state what they appreciate, and when you do it, they respond with warmth.
The good moments are common enough that you could plan around them.
Dry spells match visible reasons such as their illness, travel or workload.
Your effort is steady, and you do not feel a pull to do more to earn the next kind word.
You feel as free to relax around them as around other people you trust.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people simply express warmth rarely and unevenly, and feel more than they show.
Stress or low mood can flatten someone's expression of care for a season.
Workplaces with overloaded managers often hand out praise at random, which feels like a pattern but is only disorganisation.
common_false_positives: A friend whose attention is strong when you meet and thin between meetings, which suits both of you.
A new job where feedback is rare because everyone is busy, not because anyone is rationing it.
A relationship in therapy or recovery where good and hard weeks both come as part of real change.
discernment_questions: Roughly how many days out of ten would you call warm, and how many hurt or empty?
What would it take for the good moments to become predictable, and have you asked?
Do you work harder for approval now than when the relationship began?
Does a small kindness make you forget a month of coldness?
Would you ask a friend in your position to stay, if you heard this described?
less_concerning_if: When you ask for more consistent warmth, there is a visible effort to provide it.
The unevenness is tied to circumstances you can see and that pass.
Your life outside the relationship stays full and steady, with your own friends and goals.
more_concerning_if: The long gaps are filled with criticism and comparison, not just neutrality.
Warmth returns reliably when you threaten to leave, then fades once you stay.
You have started to doubt that you deserve more than the occasional good day.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a mental list of the good moments and replay them when things are bad.
You lower what you hope for, and treat a quiet evening as a win.
Friends see you give a great deal while receiving little, and say so.
Your own interests slip, because you save energy for the chance of the next warm episode.
Intermittent Reinforcement.repair_check: Look at whether the good treatment spreads out. Real change makes kindness frequent and ordinary, something you can count on a Tuesday. A bigger gesture after your complaint, with the gaps just as long between, is the same schedule at higher volume.
Intermittent Reinforcement.boundary_respect_check: Tell them what regular warmth would look like for you, and see what the next month holds. Are the good moments still rare and arriving as rewards, or do they turn into a daily baseline you no longer have to earn?
Intermittent Reinforcement.psychological_mechanism: Learning research has long found that rewards arriving unpredictably can keep behavior going longer than rewards that come every time. In a relationship, this may mean that uncertainty about when warmth will come keeps attention and effort fixed on the other person. The rare good moments may feel much larger against the background of the gaps, which can make leaving feel like giving up the one thing worth having.
Intermittent Reinforcement.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe a kind of hunger for the next warm moment, replaying old kind words, and pushing their own needs aside to stay in the other person's favor. Some say they feel grateful for crumbs, then ashamed of being grateful. Others describe trouble recognizing steady kindness from other people, because it seems flat beside the highs.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what helps in plain terms: 'When you tell me what I did well, I feel like I can relax. Could we try noticing the small things as they happen?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide what level of regular care you need and say it: 'I won't keep working for rare praise. I need basic kindness as the normal state, not a prize.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop trying to earn the next warm moment. Keep your effort level the same for a month and see what is offered without it.
response_options.support_seeking: Share the ratio with someone neutral, for example by writing down a month of days marked warm, neutral or cold, and show a counselor or friend the tally.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager's praise comes only now and then, ask for regular check-ins with specific criteria, and keep your own record of completed work to measure against.

Intermittent Reinforcement.boundary_script: "I've noticed I only hear good things from you once in a while, and I work very hard for those moments. I need steadier warmth, even on ordinary days. If that isn't something you can offer, I'll need to rethink how much I put in."
Intermittent Reinforcement.safety_note: By itself this is a painful emotional pattern, not a physical danger. Take it more seriously if the gaps are filled with threats, if the warm moments come only after a scare, or if you are tied to the person by money, housing or children. Then keep a record of the cycle and speak to a counselor or advocate who can help you plan your next steps while you still have your own income and contacts.
misuse_warning: Using the term to describe any uneven mood in a partner can make you read ordinary moodiness as a campaign.
Calling someone's occasional kindness 'just a reward schedule' can dismiss warmth that was real.
Intermittent Reinforcement.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Compared with Love Bombing, a heavy early flood of affection, the affection here is scarce and unpredictable. Conditional Love states the terms, such as 'I'll be warm if you obey', while this pattern never says what earns the reward. Negging mixes in insults that wear down confidence. Push-Pull swings in regular cycles of closeness and distance; this one is mostly lean, with rare warm bursts.

Trauma Bonding.short_definition: A strong attachment that forms through cycles of hurt followed by comfort from the same person, so that fear and closeness become tangled together.
Trauma Bonding.core_meaning: A strong attachment that forms through cycles of hurt followed by comfort from the same person, so that fear and closeness become tangled together.
Trauma Bonding.expanded_definition: Trauma bonding describes an attachment that grows in a relationship where harm and relief come from the same source. After a frightening or painful episode, the person who caused it is also the one who apologizes, soothes or becomes tender, and that comfort can feel unusually intense. Ordinary couples fight and make up, so a single quarrel is not this. The pattern is a repeating cycle in which the closeness after the pain is taken as proof of how deep the bond is.
Trauma Bonding.plain_language_summary: You feel most attached to the person right after they hurt you, because the same person who caused the pain is the one who comforts you.
Trauma Bonding.why_this_matters: Relief and harm come from the same person, so your strongest feeling of closeness can arrive just after the worst treatment, and then becomes a reason to stay. Knowing this can help you tell the strength of a feeling from the safety of a relationship.
what_it_is: A cycle in which a hurtful episode is followed by apology, tenderness, gifts or a heartfelt reunion from the person who caused it.
A bond that feels stronger after the worst episodes than it did before them.
A relationship where the comforter and the source of fear are one person, so there is nowhere else to turn for relief.
A shared sense that 'what we go through together proves our love', which makes the harm part of the story of the bond.
what_it_sounds_like: "I've never felt closer to anyone than I do right now," said the night after a screaming match.
"Nobody understands us. We've been through so much."
A tearful apology, a long hug and a promise, a few hours after you were threatened or humiliated.
Your own voice saying, "It's not always like this. You should see how good it is when it's good."
"If I didn't love you this much, I wouldn't get this upset."
A friend asking why you stay, and your sense that they could not understand the part after the fight.
what_it_is_not: Two people bonded by shared hardship from outside, such as caring for a sick child or surviving a disaster, where neither is the source of the pain.
A couple who quarrel loudly, apologize honestly and change something afterwards, so the same fight does not repeat.
Ordinary attachment to someone you love who has hurt you once, and who has since taken full responsibility.
The strong loyalty of family members who have been through difficult years together, with no one inflicting the harm.
A person's long-standing attachment style, which may make partings painful without anyone causing the pain.
this_may_be_it_when: The reconciliations after bad episodes feel like the most intense moments of the relationship.
You find yourself defending the person to friends while also being afraid of them.
The same kind of harm returns, and the same kind of comfort follows it.
Leaving brings a sharp physical longing, even though you know how things have been.
The person who hurt you is the only one you want when you are upset.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The hard moments are honestly acknowledged and the behavior changes afterwards.
Comfort and support come from several people, not only from the one involved in the conflict.
The hurtful incidents were few, real repair followed, and months have passed without a repeat.
Your feelings of closeness are steady and do not spike after conflict.
You feel free to leave a conversation or a room without being afraid of what follows.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people feel unusually close after an emotional reconciliation, even in healthy relationships, because strong feelings are being shared.
Grief and shared loss can bring people together in a way that feels intense and is not harmful.
Staying through a hard stretch can come from loyalty, love and practical limits such as money or children, not only from a bond to the harm.
common_false_positives: A couple in counseling who feel raw and close after an honest session about a real problem.
Soldiers, nurses or siblings who bonded through a shared ordeal.
A single serious argument, followed by sincere change, that left the relationship stronger.
discernment_questions: Do I feel closest to this person right after they have hurt me?
Is the person who comforts me the same person who caused the distress?
Has this cycle of harm and reconciliation happened more than a couple of times?
When I tell friends the good parts, do I leave out the other parts?
If someone I loved described this relationship, how worried would I be?
less_concerning_if: Harm has stopped, and the closeness has remained steady without needing a crisis.
You have other people you turn to for comfort, and you do turn to them.
The person has acknowledged specific hurts and shown lasting change.
more_concerning_if: The harm includes fear for your physical safety, threats, or humiliation in front of others.
Reconciliation follows each episode quickly and keeps you from speaking to anyone else.
You cannot picture life without the person, and the prospect of leaving brings panic.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each cycle seems to cost a bit more, and the make-up comes with higher stakes or bigger gestures.
You pull away from people who express concern, because they do not seem to see the good side.
You have left or tried to leave more than once and returned during a warm period.
Your idea of what counts as a normal bad day has shifted over time.
Trauma Bonding.repair_check: Real change here is dull and visible: the harmful episodes stop altogether, and closeness no longer depends on a crisis first. Intense reconciliation scenes that follow each new incident, with the underlying behavior unchanged, are the cycle itself and not the end of it.
Trauma Bonding.boundary_respect_check: Consider what the apology is asked to do. When you say you need the harmful behavior to stop, is the answer a different way of acting, or another emotional reunion that leaves you grateful and quiet? The second keeps the loop closed.
Trauma Bonding.psychological_mechanism: Fear and distress can heighten the need for comfort, and if comfort is available from only one person, attachment to them may deepen. Relief after a threat can feel especially strong and can be mistaken for love. Cut off from other sources of support, a person may find it harder to see the cycle, and the strength of the feeling may seem to prove the relationship is right.
Trauma Bonding.possible_impact_on_receiver: Reported experiences include being torn between dread and longing, being unable to explain to others why you stay, and shame about missing the person who hurt you. Some say they felt addicted to the reconciliation. Many describe a long period after leaving when the pull stayed strong, which surprised them and which they took, wrongly, as a sign that leaving was a mistake.

response_options.soft_clarification: If it is safe to speak, name the cycle in one sentence: 'I notice we are closest right after we have hurt each other. I want closeness without the hurt first.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide privately, with an advocate and not with the other person, what you would do if it happened again. Announcing a deadline or a consequence to someone who may react badly can raise the risk, so keep that plan to yourself and the people helping you.
response_options.disengagement: Plan any exit with care: gather documents, pick a safe place to go, and tell someone beforehand. Expect the pull to be strongest in the first weeks.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a counselor or advocate trained in relationship harm, and keep up contact with at least one person outside the relationship who knows the whole story.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss, teacher or mentor alternates harsh treatment with warmth and you feel tied to them, speak to HR, an ombuds or a mentor elsewhere before the next cycle.

Trauma Bonding.boundary_script: "I know you're sorry, and I can tell how much you mean it right now. What I need is for the apology to be followed by something different. I'd like us to talk with someone else in the room, a counselor or someone we both trust, about how these cycles go."
Trauma Bonding.safety_note: This pattern can accompany physical violence, threats, stalking, and control over money or contact, and the days around leaving are often the riskiest. Watch for escalation, strangulation, threats to kill or to harm children or pets, and weapons. Ask a domestic violence advocate to help you build a leaving plan, including where your documents, a spare phone and a go-bag will be kept.
misuse_warning: Telling someone in a hard relationship that they are 'just trauma bonded' can dismiss their real love, real reasons and practical constraints, and push them away.
Using the term for any intense make-up after a quarrel mislabels ordinary couple life as something sinister.
Trauma Bonding.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Relief Bait is the move itself: kindness placed right after harm to reset what you will tolerate. Trauma bonding is the attachment that can result when this is repeated. Intermittent Reinforcement concerns the unpredictable timing of rewards, whether or not pain precedes them. Conditional Love sets out terms; here the terms are never stated, and the bond is felt as love.

Relief Bait.short_definition: A burst of kindness placed right after hurtful treatment, so that relief takes the place of an honest reckoning with what happened.
Relief Bait.core_meaning: A burst of kindness placed right after hurtful treatment, so that relief takes the place of an honest reckoning with what happened.
Relief Bait.expanded_definition: Relief bait is the sweetness that follows a harsh moment: the gift, the soft voice, the sudden tenderness after contempt or a cold shutdown. Genuine apologies also bring kindness, so the key is what is missing. In this pattern the kindness arrives instead of naming the harm, the harm repeats, and the relief makes the next episode a little easier to absorb. One kind gesture after a quarrel proves nothing; the repeating order of hurt, then sweetness, then hurt does.
Relief Bait.plain_language_summary: Something hurtful happens, and soon afterward comes unusual kindness that never talks about what happened, so you feel relieved and let it go.
Relief Bait.why_this_matters: Each round of kindness resets what you will put up with, so the level of treatment you accept can drop without you noticing it move. You also lose the chance to have the original harm discussed.
what_it_is: Warmth, gifts or affection that arrive within hours or a day of a hurtful act, without any acknowledgment of it.
Kindness that is out of step with the way the person usually treats you, so it feels like sudden mercy.
A sequence that repeats: sharpness, then softness, then settled quiet, and then sharpness again.
A way of closing a subject by making it feel ungrateful to reopen it.
what_it_sounds_like: A bunch of flowers and "Let's not fight anymore, okay?" the morning after being called useless.
"Come here. I'm making your favorite dinner." with no mention of what was said at lunchtime.
A sudden "I booked us a weekend away!" the day after a week of silence.
"Why bring it up now? We were having such a nice evening."
A gentle back rub, a joke, and "See? We're fine."
A sweet message at 9 p.m. after a harsh one at noon, with no reference to it.
what_it_is_not: A sincere apology that names what was done, explains what will change, and comes with a gift or a kind act as an addition.
A couple who often comfort each other after tension and do so with open acknowledgement of what was said.
A person who is warm by nature and offers kindness as a gesture of care at many different times, not only after hurting you.
A move to lighten the mood after a minor disagreement that both of you consider settled.
Reaching out after an argument because they cannot bear the distance, followed by a talk the next day.
this_may_be_it_when: The kindness comes at a consistent distance after harm and is rarely seen at other times.
The hurtful behavior is never mentioned by name afterwards.
Raising the earlier incident is met with 'but I was so nice to you after'.
You notice you are grateful for ordinary decency, and the gratitude feels out of proportion.
The same kind of hurt has happened several times, each followed by the same kind of sweetness.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They name what they did before or while being kind, in specific terms.
The hurtful behavior changes, so there is less to follow with relief.
The tenderness is part of a steady pattern of warmth, not clustered around bad moments.
You can still raise the earlier incident later and have it discussed.
The harm was a single incident they have since owned up to.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often feel guilty after a harsh moment and show it through action first, planning to talk about it when they have calmed down.
Some families and cultures repair through shared food or small favors, not words.
A person embarrassed by their own behavior may find the words difficult and offer kindness as a clumsy first step.
common_false_positives: A parent who snapped at a child and then reads them a bedtime story, and later apologizes in words.
A friend who cooks you dinner after a falling out, and then talks it over at the table.
A partner whose habit of buying small gifts has nothing to do with conflict.
discernment_questions: Does the kindness come with any words about what happened?
If I bring up the earlier moment after the kindness, is it welcome or resented?
Is the sweetness more common after bad moments than at other times?
Has the hurtful behavior actually changed since the first time?
Do I feel relief, or do I feel settled and respected?
less_concerning_if: The gesture was accompanied by a plain acknowledgment, and the same hurt has not returned.
The kindness is part of how they treat you at ordinary moments too.
They are willing to discuss the incident when you raise it, even if it is uncomfortable.
more_concerning_if: The harm is getting sharper while the gestures are getting bigger.
Raising the incident after the kindness is treated as ingratitude or as ruining the mood.
The hurt includes threats, intimidation or damage to your belongings, followed by tenderness.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can tell, in the middle of the hurt, that sweetness is coming, and you may find yourself waiting for it.
Your threshold for what counts as acceptable treatment has quietly moved.
Gifts and gestures pile up while the issues behind them stay unresolved.
You find it hard to remember what the original fight was about, only how good the making-up felt.
Relief Bait.repair_check: The kindness itself tells you little, and what it is attached to tells you more. When there is change, the incident is named, in words, by them, and the behavior stops. Where only the flowers, the dinner or the soft tone appear and the hurtful act gets repeated, the gift has stood in for the repair.
Relief Bait.boundary_respect_check: After you ask them to talk about the hurtful moment before any treat or gesture, what happens? Do they sit with the topic, or does the warmth become more insistent, turning your request into the thing that spoils a nice day?
Relief Bait.psychological_mechanism: Relief after distress can feel stronger than steady comfort would, and a person may link the relief to whoever provides it. When kindness comes straight after the harm, it can blur the sense that the two events belong together, and it can make raising the harm feel mean. Repeated rounds tend to raise what feels tolerable, because the bad moments are always followed by good ones.
Relief Bait.possible_impact_on_receiver: Common accounts include guilt about staying upset when the other person is being so nice, losing track of how often it has happened, and not knowing whether to trust the gifts. Some say they began to flinch at kindness, waiting for what it covered. Others could not explain to friends what was wrong, since each good moment looked so generous from outside.

response_options.soft_clarification: Thank them for the gesture and name the missing step: 'That was kind. I'd still like to talk about what you said on Monday before we move on.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Put the order in plain terms: 'Please don't answer a hurtful moment with a gift. I'd rather you tell me what you did, and we go from there.'
response_options.disengagement: Take the gift or gesture if you want it, but keep the conversation about the incident marked as unfinished. Make a private note of what was said, and talk it over with a counselor or friend before the next conversation.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down the last three incidents and what followed each one. Show the list to a counselor or trusted friend and ask whether the order looks as odd to them as it does to you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager follows harsh criticism with praise or perks, ask for the criticism in writing with specifics, and keep your own record of both.

Relief Bait.boundary_script: "I appreciate the dinner. But it doesn't fix what you said to me earlier, and I don't want the nice evening to be where that gets dropped. Can we talk about it first? Then I'll enjoy the dinner."
Relief Bait.safety_note: Kindness that regularly follows intimidation, shoving, destroyed property or threats can be part of a controlling cycle in which things get worse over time. Watch for fear of their moods, harm that is getting more frequent, and apologies that come with pressure not to tell anyone. A domestic violence advocate can help you judge the risk and plan around it, starting with a written list of the incidents and their dates.
misuse_warning: Treating every apology gift as bait can leave you unable to accept sincere repair, and punishes people who say sorry with actions.
Telling a partner that their kindness is 'just relief bait' during a fight hands them no way to be forgiven, and can end a conversation that might have worked.
Relief Bait.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Apology Without Repair says sorry in words and changes nothing; relief bait often skips words and uses warmth. Intermittent Reinforcement is about rare, unpredictable rewards, whereas here the reward comes at a predictable moment, just after hurt. Trauma Bonding is the attachment that may grow over many cycles; relief bait is one move inside the cycle. Hoovering pulls you back after you have left, while this happens inside the relationship.

Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.short_definition: A three-stage arc in which someone is first placed on a pedestal, then steadily criticized and diminished, and finally dropped.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.core_meaning: A three-stage arc in which someone is first placed on a pedestal, then steadily criticized and diminished, and finally dropped.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.expanded_definition: This describes a whole relationship arc: a dazzling start in which you feel uniquely seen, a gradual turn in which the same qualities are criticized, and an ending that can feel abrupt or cold. Many relationships cool from early infatuation, and that alone is not this. What marks it is a turn that is sharp and out of proportion to anything you did, the criticism targets what was praised before, and people who knew the person describe the same arc with others.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.plain_language_summary: At first you are treated as perfect, then slowly as a disappointment, and then you are cast aside, as if the person you were praised for being no longer exists.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.why_this_matters: You measure the ending against the extraordinary beginning and conclude you must have caused the decline, which is also the conclusion that keeps you trying to earn the beginning back. It can be hard to grieve a relationship that changed shape so completely.
what_it_is: An opening stretch of intense admiration, fast closeness and big statements about how special you are.
A middle phase in which the same traits that were praised become faults, and comparisons or small cruelties appear.
An ending that can be sudden, cold, or carried out by silence, often with little explanation.
A sequence that some people report seeing repeat across several relationships, with similar language each time.
what_it_sounds_like: "I've never met anyone like you. It's like I've known you forever."
Later: "You used to be so interesting. What happened to you?"
"The ambition I loved is just selfishness, honestly."
Mentioning a former partner as 'crazy' who 'never appreciated me', in a story that sounds like the early praise you got.
"I don't know who you are anymore."
A final message or a block, with "I gave you everything" and no way to reply.
what_it_is_not: The normal end of infatuation, where the first intensity settles into something calmer and both people are still kind.
A relationship that ended because of real, specific problems both people could name, such as different wants about children or place.
Disappointment that goes both ways, with each person feeling let down and able to say why.
One painful break-up after a fast start, with no sign of the same arc elsewhere in the person's history.
A person ending a relationship plainly and respectfully, even if the way it ended hurts.
this_may_be_it_when: The early praise was extreme and fast, and it now reads as a script you were handed.
The turn does not follow any event, and the criticism seems to be about who you are.
Qualities they loved are now listed as flaws.
You are compared with a partner they once idealised in the same words.
The end arrives with little discussion, such as being blocked or ghosted.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The cooling follows a specific, nameable event that either of you could discuss.
They still show care and respect while saying the relationship isn't working.
You can both describe what changed, and the descriptions roughly match.
Their past relationships ended for varied reasons with no repeated arc.
The ending came with a conversation, even a hard one.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often idealise a new partner and see them more realistically over time, which can feel like loss without being a tactic.
A person who is anxious about commitment may pull away once things get serious.
Early excitement can fade when people discover real differences, and the ending can be clumsy rather than cruel.
common_false_positives: A whirlwind romance that cooled into a more ordinary one and then ended by mutual agreement.
A friendship that was close for a season and drifted apart as lives changed.
A bad break-up in which both people said unkind things at the end.
discernment_questions: Did the praise at the start feel unusually big and fast, and the criticism unusually sharp?
Can I name an event that changed things, or did the shift seem to come from nowhere?
Do the qualities they now criticize match the ones they once loved?
What do people who knew them before say about their earlier relationships?
Did the ending allow any conversation, or was I cut off?
less_concerning_if: Both of you can describe the relationship's rise and decline in similar terms.
The criticism is specific and about behavior, not about your worth.
The ending came with some honesty and without punishment.
more_concerning_if: The criticism is public, or directed at you in front of others, or shared with mutual friends.
A new person is already being praised in the same words before the old relationship is over.
The discard comes with retaliation, such as smearing you or withholding shared property.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself trying to be again the person they first described.
Their stories of former partners all follow the same shape: wonderful, then disappointing.
Your confidence drops as the criticism grows, and you hold on to memories of the start.
After the end, you replay the beginning and wonder what you did to lose it.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.repair_check: Real change would show in how they talk about the whole arc: recognizing that the early praise was larger than any person could live up to and that the criticism was out of proportion. A return to warmth with a fresh round of praise starts the first stage again.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.boundary_respect_check: Ask them to speak about specific behavior instead of general character. Notice whether they can name what happened and keep that frame, or whether the criticism widens into your whole personality and the praise from the start is quoted back as evidence of how you fell.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.psychological_mechanism: Being idealised can feel intoxicating, and a person may build part of their sense of self on it. When treatment then turns, the contrast with the early warmth tends to make people search for what they did wrong and try to recover the start. Because the beginning was real to them, they may remain hopeful long after the relationship has changed.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe whiplash, grief for a version of the relationship that may never have been stable, and doubting their own judgment about who to trust. Some say they felt discarded as if they were an object. Others describe an urge to explain themselves to the other person, long after contact had ended, in order to restore the early view.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the change directly: 'You used to say you loved how driven I am. Now it sounds like a flaw. What changed for you?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse the rewrite: 'I won't agree that I am a different person from the one you praised. If there is a problem with something I did, tell me what it was.'
response_options.disengagement: Resist the urge to win the early version back. Stop auditioning, keep your own routine, and let distance show whether the respect is still there.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the whole arc in order, including the early praise and the later criticism, and ask them what they noticed at each stage. Grief counseling can also help with the loss of the idealised start.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss or mentor praises you extravagantly and then freezes you out, keep dated records of your work and their feedback, and talk to HR or a mentor outside the relationship.

Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.boundary_script: "I was happy when you thought so highly of me, and I'm not the same person you're describing now. If you're unhappy with something I did, tell me what it was. I won't accept being told I was never who you thought I was."
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.safety_note: The arc itself is an emotional harm, not a physical one. It becomes more serious if the discard comes with a smear campaign, stalking, threats, or sudden loss of housing or income because you shared a home or business. If that begins, keep dated copies of messages, lock down your accounts, and talk to a lawyer or a domestic abuse advocate about protecting your housing and finances.
misuse_warning: Applying the label to anyone who ended a relationship after an intense beginning treats ordinary heartbreak as proof of a pattern.
Describing a former partner in these terms to friends can become a smear of its own, built from one side of the story.
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Love Bombing covers only the first stage, the overwhelming early affection, and can happen without the later criticism. Hoovering comes after the ending, when the person reappears to pull you back. Negging is a steady stream of backhanded put-downs that can occur at any point. The cycle is the whole three-part arc, from the pedestal through the decline to the drop.
